Every enterprise deploying AI agents just got a preview of the governance layer that will define the next era of enterprise software.

CrowdStrike shipped an AI Kill Switch — a mechanism to halt autonomous AI agents in production environments. In the same week, Adobe and Smartsheet embedded AI agents directly into their core products. The message is clear: agents are no longer experimental. They are shipping inside the tools your teams already use.

The governance gap is real and measurable. AI agent mentions in tech job postings have hit 14.8%, overtaking LLM references at 10.7%. The Model Context Protocol — an emerging standard for agent communication — surged from 0.3% to 4.5% in hiring mentions within a single year. Adoption is accelerating faster than most organizations have built controls for.

CrowdStrike's move is significant not because kill switches are novel, but because it signals that security vendors now see agent governance as a primary market. When your AI agents can access financial data, modify code, and trigger external workflows, the ability to halt them instantly is not a feature — it is a requirement.

For CTOs, this is the moment to audit every AI agent operating in your environment. What can each agent access? What actions can it take autonomously? Who can shut it down, and how fast?

For CEOs, the strategic question is whether your organization is deploying agents with the governance infrastructure to match — or whether you are accumulating autonomous capability without adequate control.
